extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent prosecutors and litigators handling software/business-method patents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting, prosecuting, and defending Beauregard (computer-readable-medium) patent claims covering software and other intangible inventions, including meeting statutory requirements and responding to §101/§112 challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to a tangible medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim must be directed to a tangible medium, such as a computer-readable medium or storage device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the claim language on a tangible medium (e.g., 'computer-readable medium') as the claimed subject matter to support patent-eligibility of software-related inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium must contain program instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium must contain program instructions or other software-related content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to recite that the storage medium 'contains program instructions' (or equivalent) so the claim ties the intangible functionality to content residing on a tangible medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. § 112 (definiteness and specification support)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim must be written in a way that complies with 35 U.S.C. § 112, including being definite and supported by the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claims are definite and that the specification provides written description and enablement support for claimed elements; avoid claim language that lacks specification support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and the Alice two-step test
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims must survive §101 analysis: determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea and, if so, whether it contains an inventive concept sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting, consider the Alice framework early—emphasize tangible aspects, technical improvements, or inventive concepts in the claim/specification to reduce the risk of being characterized as an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific language to define scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific language to define the scope of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise claim terms over vague or overly broad phrasing; clearly describe the tangible medium, the instructions, and any structural/functional relationships to limit ambiguity and strengthen §112/claim-construction positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include dependent claims for added definition and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider using dependent claims to further define the invention and provide additional protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft dependent claims that add concrete limitations, alternative embodiments, and fallback positions to preserve claim scope through prosecution or litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct thorough prior art searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct thorough prior art searches to identify potential issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for prior art that could affect novelty, obviousness, or claim-eligibility; use the results to tailor claim scope and draft supporting specification content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft claims that are specific, clear, and concise
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims that are specific, clear, and concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity and concision aid examiner understanding, reduce §112 risks, and strengthen enforcement—avoid unnecessary functional/formal obfuscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the specification provides adequate support
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the specification provides adequate support for the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include examples, embodiments, and detailed descriptions of how the program instructions operate on the medium to satisfy written description and enablement requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond promptly to office actions and address objections/rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond promptly to office actions and address any objections or rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely, substantive responses that amend claims, argue statutory compliance, or present evidence can preserve claimability during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common pitfalls in Beauregard claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Common pitfalls to avoid: using overly broad or vague language; failing to comply with 35 U.S.C. § 112; not providing adequate support in the specification; ignoring prior art and potential validity issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively prevent these mistakes by using precise claim language, robust specification disclosure, and careful prior-art-based claim drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue tangible-medium focus to defend §101 challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: When defending against invalidity challenges, argue that the claim is directed to a tangible medium and therefore is patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame arguments to the court or examiner emphasizing the physical storage/medium aspects and how the claimed invention is not merely an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize claim language and specification support in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the specific language used in the claim to define the scope of the invention and highlight the support provided in the specification for the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claim-construction briefs and specification citations to show that claim elements are concrete and supported, countering §112 and §101 attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use expert testimony to show novelty and non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Use expert testimony to demonstrate the novelty and non-obviousness of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In litigation, expert evidence can explain technical differences over prior art and whether claimed features represent an inventive concept under Alice step two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement requires meeting each claim element
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed in a patent infringement case, the patent owner must demonstrate that the accused product or process meets each element of the Beauregard claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare element-by-element infringement analyses, claim charts, and factual evidence showing the accused product contains the claimed medium/content or equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay informed of evolving case law and its impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent court decisions continue to shape Beauregard claims; stay informed about developments (e.g., In re Beauregard, State Street, Bilski, Alice, Vanda) and their implications for §101 and claim drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor jurisprudence and adapt drafting and litigation strategies accordingly—cite favorable precedent and distinguish adverse decisions when possible.
